preamble: 12 clues have two letter counts; the first count refers to one of a pair of 'Lookalikes' (arrived at by solving the clue) and the second to the other half of the pair (the entry to be made in the grid). These have all appeared in our Lookalikes slots during 2014. Letters of these entries not intersecting with other clue answers are: AAAAA CC DDDD EEEEEEE F G HH IIIIII K LLLLL M N OOOO PP RRRRR SS TTT UUUU W YY Z

clue.text: Money corrupted the law

indicators.note: something corrupted has been twisted out of its proper form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cynical complaint that cash has bent the legal system.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence, but 'Money' is the definition and 'corrupted' tells you to rearrange the two words that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealth is a stock of riches or possessions, so it serves as a plain synonym for cash and assets.

clue.text: Lay out gusset for thong's mid-section

indicators.note: a mid-section is the middle part of something, so the letters sit inside the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Sewing instructions: place the gusset for the middle of a thong.
explanation.walkthrough: A gusset is the reinforcing panel in the crotch of underwear, which makes 'mid-section' sound like a garment part rather than a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To set forth is to present or explain something in order, which is what laying out an argument or plan means.

clue.text: City gets sod all raised by Colonel North

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters lifts them so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: sod all is British slang for nothing, which is nil
Col is the standard abbreviation for Colonel
N is the compass abbreviation for North

explanation.surface: A city ends up with nothing, thanks to Colonel Oliver North of the Iran-Contra affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonel North' reads as one person, Oliver North, but it splits into two abbreviations. 'Sod all' is British slang for nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Lincoln is a cathedral city in the East Midlands of England, so it fits the bare definition of a city.

clue.text: High seas fun, late, is risky for lovers

definitions.note: an adjective phrase defining a noun phrase: what lovers do that is risky

indicators.note: high spirits or being high means being out of one's normal state, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written
late can mean former, as in the late husband, and a former partner is an ex

explanation.surface: A late-night holiday romance on a cruise could be dangerous for the couple involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High seas' looks like a single phrase, but 'High' is the signal and 'seas fun' is the material; 'late' gives EX in its sense of former.
explanation.definitionFit: Sex without protection carries the danger of disease or pregnancy, which is the risk the clue says lovers face.

clue.text: A grunt? No, a windy tree-dweller (9);

definitions.note: defines the clue's own answer, ORANGUTAN; the grid takes its lookalike

indicators.note: windy suggests being blown about, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hears a noise from a tree and decides it was not a grunt but flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: This Christmas puzzle has a Private Eye Lookalikes theme: the clue gives ORANGUTAN, and the grid takes the celebrity it supposedly resembles, the glamour model Katie Price.
explanation.definitionFit: Orangutans are great apes of Borneo and Sumatra that live almost entirely in the forest canopy.

clue.text: Country's leader intervenes in this, or disaster? It won't fly

indicators.note: to intervene is to come between, so one letter goes into the middle of the others
a disaster is things going badly wrong, so the letters end up in a wrecked order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of Country

explanation.surface: A national leader steps into a crisis and asks whether this will become a disaster that never takes off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a politician's crisis, but the definition is a riddle at the end: the bird is famously flightless.
explanation.definitionFit: The ostrich is the largest living bird and cannot get airborne, so a creature that never takes wing describes it.

clue.text: Sticking points in chopper, as Hitler was prone to do

definitions.text: as Hitler was prone to do
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the verb: what he habitually did

indicators.note: sticking something in a thing pushes it inside, so some letters go within another word

parts.note: an axe is a chopper
compass points: N, N and E, together the bearing north-north-east

explanation.surface: Sticking points in a negotiation with a dictator who wielded the axe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticking points' looks like one phrase meaning obstacles, but it splits: compass points are stuck inside the chopper. The British spelling with a final E is used for the verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitler seized Austria and the Sudetenland by annexing them, taking territory and adding it to Germany by force.

clue.text: Steaming in, pissed — "sex for one is a chore"

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order
putting one thing in place of another is to swap it for that thing

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for sex, as on forms
one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A drunk staggering home declares that solo sex is a tedious job.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap one of the two Is in the first two words for S, then rearrange all ten letters. 'Steaming' and 'pissed' are both British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: An assignment is a task that has been allotted to someone, so a chore or piece of set work fits it.

clue.text: Getting laid here for almost the very last time could make fleshpot race

definitions.text: Getting laid here for almost the very last time

indicators.note: the letters could be made into something else, so they are refashioned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boast about sex at a brothel race meeting, maybe for the last time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting laid' sounds sexual, but the body is laid out. 'Almost' is fair because burial or cremation, the truly final resting, comes afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapel of rest is a funeral director's room where the dead are laid out for viewing before the funeral.

clue.text: Parrot — or a tit I'm wobbling?

indicators.note: something wobbling is unsteady and will not hold its shape, so the letters move around

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is it a parrot, or a bird of the tit family losing its balance?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parrot' and 'tit' both look like birds, but the first is a noun for a copier and the second is just raw letters. Here 'or' does double duty as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A parrot, figuratively, is someone who repeats others' words without thought, which is an imitator or mimic.

clue.text: It's thick-skinned like certain Irishmen

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a citrus fruit with a thick peel
second meaning: belonging to the loyalist Protestant order of Northern Ireland

explanation.walkthrough: The Orange Order is a Protestant fraternal organisation strong in Northern Ireland; 'thick-skinned' also hints that its members are unbending.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit has a tough rind, and Orangemen are the loyalist Protestants who march each July in Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Immunity of drug-taking former member getting into trouble

indicators.note: taking something in holds it within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: E is ecstasy, the drug

indicators.note: trouble is disorder, so these letters are thrown into a muddle

parts.note: a Member of Parliament
taken as written
an ex is a former partner, and ex- means former

explanation.surface: A drug-taking former MP escapes prosecution despite getting into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting into trouble' reads as a single idea, but 'into' is the material and the rest is the signal. The drug is inside the former member.
explanation.definitionFit: An exemption frees someone from a duty or liability that others face, which is what immunity from prosecution means.

clue.text: see 14ac.
(&13dn.) Actress's mobile kept in pee-hole (8,5);

definitions.note: defines the clue's own answer, PENELOPE KEITH; the grid takes its lookalike

indicators.note: something mobile moves freely, so the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An actress's phone gets stuck somewhere very unfortunate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone, but it is the signal. The clue gives PENELOPE KEITH; under the preamble's Lookalikes theme the grid takes the cross-dressing potter she supposedly resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope Keith is the English star of The Good Life and To the Manor Born, an example of a stage and television performer.

clue.text: Beg to have oral sex — bishop finished with a joint

parts.note: slang for performing oral sex on someone
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
ended means finished
the knee is a joint of the leg

explanation.surface: A bishop pleads for sex, then finishes off by smoking a spliff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A joint' suggests a cannabis cigarette, but it is a body part. 'Beg' is the definition, and 'to' only links it.
explanation.definitionFit: Kneeling is the traditional posture of a supplicant, so the idiom means to plead humbly or implore.

clue.text: Planners screech "M&S about to go bust!"

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters are rebuilt in another order
something told to go leaves, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
c is short for circa, about; one C leaves
taken as written: Marks and Spencer, the British high-street chain

explanation.surface: Business planners shriek that Marks and Spencer is about to go bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to go bust' reads as a headline, but it is three signals: 'about' is C, 'to go' removes it, 'bust' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Schemers are people who make plans, especially crafty or secret ones, so they are planners with a sly edge.

clue.text: Model film star's orchestra not accented, fruit (5,5);

definitions.note: defines the clue's own answer, HALLE BERRY; the grid takes its lookalike

parts.note: the Hallé is a Manchester orchestra; drop the accent from its name
a berry is a fruit

explanation.surface: A movie star's orchestra plays without emphasis, plus some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives HALLE BERRY; under the preamble's Lookalikes theme the grid takes the singer she supposedly resembles. The Hallé is Manchester's symphony orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: Halle Berry was a fashion model and beauty queen before becoming an Oscar-winning Hollywood actress.

clue.text: Netanyahu is one old-time PM casting out dead

indicators.note: casting something out throws it away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: Benjamin Disraeli was Victorian Prime Minister
D is the abbreviation for dead, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A comparison of Benjamin Netanyahu with a Victorian prime minister who threw out the dead.
explanation.walkthrough: The old-time PM is Benjamin Disraeli, Victorian Prime Minister; removing D, the abbreviation for dead, leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Netanyahu is the Prime Minister of Israel, so he is an example of a citizen of that country.

clue.text: see 64dn.
Piss almost taken out of Brenda, say, for her grand self-referencing?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, an example of the royal, so her piss is the royal one
a wee is a piss

explanation.surface: Someone takes the piss out of the Queen for her pompous habit of talking about herself.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II; 'taken out of Brenda, say' fixes whose wee it is. 'Taking the piss' is British slang for mocking.
explanation.definitionFit: Monarchs traditionally say 'we' instead of 'I', a plural pronoun used grandly to refer to one sovereign person.

clue.text: WC involved with a penile dysfunction — use a rubber?

indicators.note: a dysfunction is something not working properly, so the letters are out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man with erectile trouble in the toilet wonders whether to put on a condom.
explanation.walkthrough: A rubber is a condom in American slang but an eraser in British English, and the eraser is the sense wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Using an eraser on a page rubs off the marks, leaving it wiped clean of writing.

clue.text: see 48dn.
"Bow — one has a record collection"

parts.note: an arch is a bow shape
one is I, the Roman numeral
the contraction 've, as in 'I've', means has or have

explanation.surface: A quoted remark: someone bows and says one of them owns a collection of vinyl records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record collection' suggests a pile of LPs, but it means a store of documents. 'Has' becomes the short form 've.
explanation.definitionFit: An archive is a collection of historical documents or records kept for reference.

clue.text: What greedy MP expense-claimers do — i.e. rank badly

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A jab at MPs who fiddled their expenses: they are greedy and rank poorly in public esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: This refers to the 2009 British scandal over MPs' expense claims. 'Rank' looks like a verb for rating them, but it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To rake in money is to gather large sums easily, as if scooping it up with a garden tool, which greedy claimers did.

clue.text: Pulsating TV in for repair (front cover wedged inside)

indicators.note: a thing wedged inside is jammed into the middle of something else
something in for repair is broken and will be put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written
a bra covers the front of the chest

explanation.surface: A flickering television sent for repair, with its front casing jammed inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front cover' sounds like a panel of the TV set, but it is underwear for the front of the body. 'Pulsating' looks like a fault, yet it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Vibrant means full of energy and life, throbbing with activity, which matches something that pulsates.

clue.text: Put down which Monica got as a parting shot from Clinton?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to set something down or place it

definitions.text: which Monica got as a parting shot from Clinton
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the stain Bill Clinton left on Monica Lewinsky's blue dress

explanation.walkthrough: The second half refers to the 1998 scandal in which DNA evidence on Monica Lewinsky's dress proved her affair with President Clinton; 'parting shot' is a crude pun on ejaculation.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to lay something down; as a noun it means matter left behind, such as a sediment or a stain.

clue.text: Royal baby mould via singing comedian (6;6)

definitions.note: defines the clue's own answer, GEORGE FORMBY; the grid takes its lookalike

parts.note: Prince George, born 2013, the son of Prince William
to form is to mould
by means via, as in travelling by train

explanation.surface: A royal infant is shaped by a funny man who sings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal baby' looks like the definition but is wordplay for Prince George. The clue gives GEORGE FORMBY; under the preamble's Lookalikes theme the grid takes the UKIP leader he supposedly resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: George Formby was a 1930s and 1940s British entertainer famous for comic songs on the ukulele, such as When I'm Cleaning Windows.

clue.text: Resistance evident in dire Blair event — head off, it's off-topic

indicators.note: with the head taken off, the first letter is gone
being evident within something means showing up inside it
dire means dreadful, so the letters are left in a dreadful jumble

parts.note: the two words with the first letter of the surname removed
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Opposition is plain at some disastrous Tony Blair occasion, and someone storms off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head off' sounds like leaving, but it removes the first letter of Blair before the rearrangement. Resistance is R in physics.
explanation.definitionFit: Something irrelevant has no bearing on the matter being discussed, so it strays from the subject in hand.

clue.text: Scandal-monger? Piss off, piss off!

parts.note: piss off is a rude British way of telling someone to go away

indicators.note: something gone off has gone wrong, so the letters are put out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells a rumour-spreader twice over to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated phrase looks like emphasis, but each one works differently: the first is a command, the second is the word plus a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A gossip is a person who habitually spreads rumours and tittle-tattle about others, a scandal-spreading busybody.

clue.text: Actress has screwed, with credit, many a time, as the Bard would put it

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted, so the letters are turned into another order

parts.note: taken as written
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit

parts.words: many a time, as the Bard would put it
parts.note: oft is the old word for often, used by Shakespeare

explanation.surface: Gossip about an actress who has slept around often, told in Shakespearean language.
explanation.walkthrough: Peggy Ashcroft was a celebrated British stage actress famed for Shakespeare roles, which makes the Bard reference apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Peggy Ashcroft was a leading English performer of stage and screen, so she is an example of the given category.

clue.text: The dummy getting fired for failing to elevate Westminster? (3,6);

definitions.text: The dummy getting fired for failing to elevate Westminster?
definitions.note: defines the clue's own answer, GUY FAWKES; the grid takes its lookalike

parts.note: surface reading: a ventriloquist's dummy losing its job
setter's reading: the effigy burnt on 5 November because the 1605 Gunpowder Plot failed to blow up Parliament

explanation.surface: A puppet is sacked because it could not lift Parliament's standing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's answer is GUY FAWKES, whose effigy, the guy, is burnt on Bonfire Night. This Christmas puzzle has a Private Eye Lookalikes theme, so the grid takes the cleric he supposedly resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: Fawkes was caught guarding gunpowder under Parliament in 1605; Britons still burn a stuffed effigy of him every November.

clue.text: Royal Bruce, the animated female lead? (8,5);

definitions.note: defines the clue's own answer, PRINCESS FIONA; the grid takes its lookalike

parts.note: a princess is a royal
Fiona Bruce, the BBC newsreader, gives her first name

explanation.surface: A royal named Bruce cast as the cartoon heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives PRINCESS FIONA, heroine of the Shrek films. This Christmas puzzle has a Private Eye Lookalikes theme, so the grid takes the singer she supposedly resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: Princess Fiona is the ogre-princess heroine of the DreamWorks cartoon films, the leading woman of an animated movie.

clue.text: Simpson's boss married Scotland's bard, formally (2,5);

definitions.note: defines the clue's own answer, MR BURNS; the grid takes its lookalike

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet, given formally as initial and surname

explanation.surface: Homer Simpson's employer weds the poet of Scotland in a formal ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives MR BURNS, Homer's boss in The Simpsons. This Christmas puzzle has a Private Eye Lookalikes theme, so the grid takes the politician he supposedly resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: Montgomery Burns owns the Springfield nuclear plant where Homer Simpson works, making him that cartoon character's employer.

clue.text: Salmond's twitter: "Blair broadcast off air"

indicators.note: off means removed, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
the three letters that come off
the ether is the airwaves, the medium a broadcast travels through

explanation.surface: Alex Salmond tweets that a Tony Blair programme should be taken off air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twitter' suggests the social network but means chatter. Alex Salmond was then the SNP leader, so the definition calls for a Scottish word.
explanation.definitionFit: Blether is a Scots noun for idle talk or prattle, so a Scotsman's chattering is blether.

clue.text: Paper T-shirt front and tie arse's sporting

indicators.note: the front of something is where it begins, so only its first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of T-shirt

indicators.note: sporting can mean playing about, so the letters frolic into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive S included

explanation.surface: A tabloid reports someone wearing just a T-shirt top, with a tie round their bum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' looks like a newspaper heading the story, but it means an academic essay.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a formal written study of a subject, the sort of paper a scholar would publish.

clue.text: Orange order entering to secure Ian's heart

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the letters are put into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart of something is its centre, so only the middle letter is used

parts.note: the middle letter of Ian

explanation.surface: The Orange Order recruiting Ian Paisley at its core.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orange order' reads as the Northern Irish Protestant body, but 'Orange' is the definition and 'order' the signal. Ian Paisley was a leading Ulster loyalist.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangerine is a small, loose-skinned citrus fruit related to the mandarin, a kind of orange.

clue.text: Support a bit of a pig's board activity

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
gammon is cured meat from the hind leg of a pig

explanation.surface: Someone supports a pig's part in some activity on a board.
explanation.walkthrough: Gammon is a cut of cured pork, the hind leg of a pig, common in British cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Backgammon is an ancient two-player game played with dice and counters on a board of triangular points.

clue.text: Jagger, back of cab, in a pissed state?

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of cab

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order

parts.note: taken as written
CA is the postal abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: A Jagger is in the back of a taxi, drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jagger' first suggests Mick, but the answer is his first wife, Bianca Jagger.
explanation.definitionFit: Bianca Jagger, the Nicaraguan-born activist, was married to Mick, so she is one person bearing that surname.

clue.text: Balls stuck to right of chin, a sad victim of a dominatrix?

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for an adjective: describes the state of such a victim

indicators.note: sad can mean sorry or poor in quality, so the letters are in a sorry state

parts.note: taken as written
Ed Balls was then Labour's shadow chancellor

explanation.surface: Testicles pinned to someone's chin in a pitiful bondage scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like testicles, but it is the politician Ed Balls, who goes to the right of the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dominatrix's submissive partner is often bound in fetters, so being chained describes such a captive.

clue.text: Maybe Miliband acted … to secure a 25% share of vote

indicators.note: securing something holds it fast within, so the letters go inside

parts.note: did is the past tense of do, so it means acted
taken as written

indicators.note: a quarter of a four-letter word is one letter, here the first

parts.note: the first letter of vote, a quarter of its four letters

explanation.surface: Miliband did something to win a quarter of the vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks an example: there are two Miliband brothers, Ed and David, and the 2010 Labour leadership vote between them was famously close.
explanation.definitionFit: David Miliband, former Foreign Secretary, is one of two well-known brothers with that surname, so he is an example.

clue.text: see 42ac.
Idiot messed with Sly's hard, firm state

indicators.note: something messed with has been tampered with and disordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fool picks a fight with Sylvester Stallone, whose tough condition is legendary.
explanation.walkthrough: Sly is Sylvester Stallone's nickname, and his muscle-bound image makes 'hard, firm' look like a description of him.
explanation.definitionFit: Solidity is the quality of being solid, hard and rigid rather than soft or liquid, a sturdy condition.

clue.text: (& 40ac.) They're served by court activity? Bollocks!

parts.note: a game played on a court
both are British slang for testicles, and for nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at being served papers by a court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served by court' suggests a legal summons, but the court is a sports one. Bollocks is British slang for testicles, and an exclamation of disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis each point starts with a player serving the ball over the net, so the balls are what is served.

clue.text: Nevertheless, as timely grandfathers go, not a complete arse

parts.note: but means nevertheless, however
grandfather clocks go tick-tock, and tock is the second half of the sound

explanation.surface: An old man who keeps good time is, all the same, a bit of an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: The grandfathers are long-case clocks, not elderly men. 'Not a complete arse' is fair because one cheek is only half the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A buttock is one of the two rounded cheeks of the bottom, so a single one is only part of the whole rear.

clue.text: Going topless, pulls — hangover results

indicators.note: with no top, the first letter of the word is lost

parts.note: to heave is to pull hard

explanation.surface: A night out where someone strips off and pulls, followed by a sore head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulls' is British slang for picking someone up, and 'hangover' suggests the morning after; but the definition is literal, something that hangs over.
explanation.definitionFit: Eaves are the lower edges of a roof that project beyond the wall, literally overhanging the building.

clue.text: Verbose book, bizarrely blue

parts.note: vol is short for volume, a book

indicators.note: done bizarrely means done oddly, so the letters land in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wordy book that is oddly smutty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like a description of the book's content, meaning risqué, but it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Voluble means talking fluently and at length, so it is a close synonym for wordy or long-winded.

clue.text: Alongside cops collectively using strong-arm tactics

parts.note: by means beside or alongside
the police force is the body of officers taken together

explanation.surface: Police officers banding together and using heavy-handed methods.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface depicts police brutality, which is what the answer describes too, but it is made from a preposition and a collective noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something by force means achieving it through physical power or coercion, the essence of strong-arm methods.

clue.text: see 72dn.
(& 21ac.) Foreign (permissive type) johnny

parts.note: an example of a foreign language or nationality, to a Briton
one who lets or allows things, a permissive person

explanation.surface: A foreign, sexually liberal man called Johnny.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnny is British slang for a condom, not a man's name. 'Foreign' standing for one nationality is a loose example.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for a condom; the older phrase reflects the English habit of blaming sexual matters on the French.

clue.text: Blue shade of political party suffering reverse (put in somewhere to rest)

indicators.note: something put in is placed inside another thing

parts.note: a cot is a small bed

indicators.note: a reverse is a setback, and suffering one turns things backwards

parts.note: Lab is the abbreviation for the Labour Party

explanation.surface: A party in trouble with blue, the Tory colour, laid to rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the Conservative colour in Britain, which makes 'political party' look like the Tories, though the letters come from Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobalt is a deep, vivid blue pigment made from cobalt salts, so it names one particular hue of that colour.

clue.text: Which, in fact, came to Thatcher's rescue? Thank Ed's fall out

definitions.text: Which, in fact, came to Thatcher's rescue?

indicators.note: things that fall out tumble from their places and land in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, while also forming part of the signal

explanation.surface: A political taunt that Ed Miliband's collapse would save the Tories, as an old war once saved Thatcher.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1982 war over these British islands revived Margaret Thatcher's popularity before the 1983 election. 'Fall' serves twice, as fodder and in the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Victory in the 1982 South Atlantic war rescued Thatcher's low poll ratings, so the islands literally saved her premiership.

clue.text: Shabby stuff, including the end of Bieber's recorded item

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so one letter goes inside

parts.note: tack is cheap, shoddy goods, the root of tacky

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is used

parts.note: the final letter of Bieber

explanation.surface: Tacky merchandise with a Justin Bieber recording thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a sneer at Bieber's music as cheap stuff, but his name supplies only its final letter.
